title: Tenant-aware cache warmup and compact KV-slice allocator for request-level prefix reuse
creator: María Alvarez
description: Problem: We see repeated short-lived request prefixes across tenants that are hot for seconds but evicted by the current slab allocator and LRU windows, causing expensive re-population and extra decoding steps. This increases p99 latency and GPU memory churn for small chat workloads. Goal: implement an opportunistic, tenant-aware warmup layer combined with a compact KV-slice allocator to increase prefix reuse across requests and reduce GPU memory fragmentation without increasing steady-state resident memory by more than 5%. The feature should be safe for multi-tenant pools, respect per-tenant isolation policies (no cross-tenant data leakage), and be reversible if it causes regressions.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end test demonstrating ≥30% reduction in repeated prefix fetches for short-lived conversational prefixes on our internal chat workload suite
p99 generation latency decreases by ≥8% on benchmark workload A with no more than 5% increase in average resident GPU memory usage
No cross-tenant KV visibility in unit and integration tests; audit logs present for warmup activity
Feature gate and runtime flags to disable warmup or compact allocator per pool/tenant
Automated canary in staging that runs for 48h without increased error rates before rollout
design_notes: Warmup heuristics: maintain a short-lived, bloom-filter-backed 'micro-warm' index per tenant that records recent prefix fingerprints (TTL default 30s). When a request arrives and a prefix match is found in the micro-warm index, proactively attach the KV slices to the request via a fast path, avoiding a full remote fetch.

Scoring: prioritize warmups by a tenant-aware hotness score that includes recency, token overlap with current request, and tenant priority tier. Hotness score bounded to avoid noisy tenants from thrashing GPU memory.

Compact KV-slice allocator: pack variable-length KV fragments into contiguous GPU slabs using a run-length aware packing strategy with per-slab occupancy bitmaps. Slabs support a lightweight compaction pass during low-util periods to reduce fragmentation.

Eviction coordination: integrate warmup with existing global eviction so that warmed slices are considered 'soft-resident' and can be demoted first under memory pressure. Soft-resident flag is ephemeral and never persisted across node restarts.

Safety: all warmup data is namespaced by tenant; allocator metadata never contains user prompt content in plain text, only fingerprints and slice descriptors. KMS/HSM keys not involved because this is metadata only; confirm with security for compliance note.

API and metrics: expose per-pool warmup hit rate, warmup CPU/GPU overhead, micro-warm index size, and compaction time. Runtime flags: warmup_enabled, micro_warm_ttl_sec, slab_compaction_window_sec, tenant_hotness_threshold.

Trade-offs: warmup reduces remote fetches but increases short-lived GPU allocations and bookkeeping; compacting can cause extra compute during low load. We will gate compaction during peak hours by default.
rollout_plan: Feature behind runtime flag and per-pool config; default off for existing production pools
Stage 1: Deploy to internal staging pools with synthetic chat workloads for 48h monitor
Stage 2: Canary rollout to 5% traffic on low-latency public pool A with observation window 72h
Stage 3: Gradual 25% → 50% → 100% rollout with rollback on metric thresholds (p99 latency increase >3% or error rate increase >0.1%)
Rollback plan: flip runtime flag off, drain warmed slices over 5 minutes, and return to baseline allocator behavior
testing_plan: Unit tests for micro-warm index insert/evict and tenant namespace separation
Integration tests: simulate mixed-tenant traffic, verify no cross-tenant warmups and validate eviction order semantics
Performance tests: run benchmark suite A/B with and without warmup to measure latency, GPU memory, and throughput
Chaos test: OOM injection during compaction to validate graceful demotion and monitoring alerts
Security test: static scan of metadata paths and a quick review with security team to ensure no content persistence
